2.evidence_source: Study 1 sought to examine the factor structure, internal consistency, convergent validity, and incremental validity of a state version of the BAS-2 (hereafter referred to as the SBAS-2), as well as sex differences in state BA.
2._section_summary: Study 1 evaluated a state version of the BAS-2 (referred to as the SBAS-2), focusing on its factor structure, internal consistency, convergent validity, and incremental validity. The study also examined sex differences in state body appreciation and hypothesized that state BA would correlate positively with life satisfaction and self-esteem, negatively with BMI, and that men and women would show similar levels of state BA.

3.evidence_source: The 10-item Body Appreciation Scale-2 (BAS-2; Tylka & Wood-Barcalow, 2015) was used as the basis for the SBAS-2.
3._section_summary: This Measures section describes instruments used to assess state body appreciation and related constructs: a state-adapted version of the 10-item BAS-2 (SBAS-2), the six-item Body Image States Scale (BISS), the five-item Satisfaction With Life Scale (SWLS), the Single-Item Self-Esteem Scale (SISE), and calculation of BMI from self-reported height and weight. The section reports internal consistency for some scales (e.g., BISS α = .84; SWLS α = .94) but provides no sample demographics, sample size, survey mode, country, or any correlations between body appreciation and BMI; no explicit study numbering is provided.

4.evidence_source: Consistent with the development of the BAS-2, factor analysis was performed separately by sex (Tylka & Wood-Barcalow, 2015).
4._section_summary: This section reports validation analyses for the SBAS-2/BAS-2 conducted separately for male and female subsamples, including EFA results (one factor for each sex; men eigenvalue = 7.73 explaining 77.28% variance; women eigenvalue = 7.96 explaining 79.60% variance) and very high internal consistency (α = .97 for both sexes). Between-group t-tests showed no significant item or scale differences between men and women (all ps ≥ .13; mean scale t(244) = 0.14, p = .89). Convergent and incremental validity analyses indicate SBAS-2 correlates positively with life satisfaction and self-esteem and is inversely associated with BMI, though numeric BMI correlations are presented in Table 2 and not reported in this text.

6._section_summary: Exploratory factor analyses were conducted separately for male and female subsamples and each yielded a single-factor solution for the SBAS-2 with very high internal consistency (Cronbach's alpha = .97 for both men and women). No significant item or total-score differences were found between men and women (t(244) = 0.14, p = .89). Correlational results (Table 2) show SBAS-2 positively associated with life satisfaction and self-esteem and inversely associated with BMI (men r = −.31; women r = −.34).

7._section_summary: Study 2 tested whether the SBAS-2 could detect momentary changes in body appreciation by asking participants to complete the SBAS-2 after imagining brief scenarios manipulating perceived acceptance of their body by family, friends, romantic partners, or the media. The manipulation was based on prior work linking perceived acceptance from important others to body appreciation and mirrors methods used to validate other state measures.

8.evidence_source: These scenarios were presented in random order, and participants completed the SBAS-2 after reading and imagining each situation.
8._section_summary: This Methods section describes a single study recruiting 105 participants (45 female, 60 male) via Amazon's MTurk. Participants ranged from 18 to 69 years (M=34.28) and were 80.8% White; they completed six imagined scenarios and the SBAS-2 after each scenario.
